And if you're feeling more weekend than weeknight, my <a href="https://whatsgabycooking.com/thai-style-baby-back-ribs/">Thai Style Baby Back Ribs</a> are right there with you.</p>

<h2 id="why-i-love-this-recipe"   class="wp-block-heading">Why I love this Recipe </h2>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Here’s the deal - you’ll need 1: a rice base for this dish. 2: some incredible protein in the form of pork that comes with the best sticky sauce. And 3: a few garnishes to really seal the deal. It’s incredible. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Made with pork tenderloin, this is one of those meals that can be made in no time and I promise you, it’ll be on the weekly rotation for dinners. Pork tenderloin can be prepared a number of ways and is flavorful, lean and easy to cook. It’s quick too.  Two things to keep in mind when you’re cooking tenderloin: You’re going to be looking for an internal cooking temperature of 145° F. Once it’s cooked, you’ll want to let the pork rest for a few minutes to let the juice redistribute.  This will help make the pork as delicious as possible and extra juicy. Check out <a href="http://pork.org" target="_blank" rel="noopener">pork.org</a> for more tips and trips to making perfect pork dishes every time </p>

<h2 id="substitutions-swaps"   class="wp-block-heading" >Substitutions & Swaps</h2>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading">🐖 Pork</h4>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Pork tenderloin (called for)</strong> - The leanest, fastest cook</li>



<li><strong>Boneless pork loin chops</strong> - Cube and sear; same cook time</li>



<li><strong>Ground pork</strong> - Brown and crumble for a faster build</li>



<li><strong>Boneless skinless chicken thighs</strong> - Cut into ½-inch strips, marinate the same way</li>



<li><strong>Extra-firm tofu</strong> - Press 30 minutes, cube, dust in cornstarch and sear hard</li>
</ul>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading">🌶️ Heat</h4>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Sambal oelek</strong> - Cleaner heat than chili garlic sauce, less garlic forward</li>



<li><strong>Sriracha</strong> - Sweeter and sharper, reduce honey by 1 tablespoon to keep it balanced</li>



<li><strong>Gochujang</strong> - Korean swap, deeper fermented umami</li>



<li><strong>Reduce to 1.5 to 2 tbsp</strong> - Several readers flag the full 4 tablespoon as too spicy for kids; cut for a milder bowl</li>



<li><strong>Mild ketchup-based glaze</strong> - For heat-averse eaters: swap chili sauce for 4 tablespoon ketchup + 1 teaspoon paprika</li>
</ul>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading">🍯 Sweetener</h4>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Maple syrup</strong> - Same 1:1 swap, cleaner sweetness, slightly less sticky</li>



<li><strong>Brown sugar (½ cup)</strong> - Deeper caramel notes, dissolve in 2 tablespoon warm water before adding</li>



<li><strong>Honey-mustard blend</strong> - Honey + 1 tablespoon Dijon for tangy variation</li>
</ul>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading">🍚 Rice or Base</h4>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Jasmine rice</strong> - Aromatic, classic pairing</li>



<li><strong>Short-grain sushi rice</strong> - Stickier, gives a more bowl-style hold</li>



<li><strong>Cauliflower rice</strong> - Low-carb option, sauté quickly with sesame oil</li>



<li><strong>Lo mein noodles</strong> - Toss with the glaze for a stir-fry-style version</li>
</ul>



<h4 class="wp-block-heading">🥒 Garnishes</h4>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Quick-pickled red onion</strong> - Adds tang in place of cucumber</li>



<li><strong>Crispy fried shallots</strong> - Storebought is fine, adds crunch</li>



<li><strong>Toasted peanuts or cashews</strong> - For nuttiness and texture</li>



<li><strong>Lime wedges</strong> - Bright finish that cuts through the sticky glaze</li>



<li><strong>Soft-boiled egg</strong> - 6 minutes, jammy yolk, the move when you want this for breakfast</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="%f0%9f%90%96%f0%9f%8d%af%f0%9f%8c%b6%ef%b8%8f-tips-tricks-for-the-best-sticky-glazed-pork-rice-bowls"   class="wp-block-heading">🐖🍯🌶️ Tips & Tricks for the Best Sticky Glazed Pork Rice Bowls</h2>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph"><em>Restaurant-style sticky glaze, pork that's juicy in 15 minutes flat</em></p>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Cut the pork tenderloin against the grain.</strong> Look for the muscle fibers and slice perpendicular. Cuts that go with the grain stay tough no matter how perfect your sear.</li>



<li><strong>Slice the strips uniform thickness.</strong> ¼-inch strips at 3 inches long is the move. Anything thicker overcooks on the outside before the inside hits 145°F.</li>



<li><strong>Pull the pork at 145°F internal temp.</strong> Use a meat thermometer if you have one. Pork carries over 5°F as it rests, so 145 in the pan is 150 by the time it hits the bowl. Past that and it's dry.</li>



<li><strong>Rest the pork 3 minutes before glazing.</strong> Slap it on a plate while you build the glaze. Resting redistributes juice into the meat instead of onto the cutting board.</li>



<li><strong>Sear in batches no bigger than a single layer.</strong> Crowding drops the pan temp 100°F and you'll end up with steamed gray pork. Two or three rounds, even if it feels slow.</li>



<li><strong>Get the pan hot before the pork goes in.</strong> Cast iron over medium-high until you see the oil shimmer and just start to smoke. That's when you build crust.</li>



<li><strong>Build the glaze in the same pan.</strong> All that browned fond at the bottom is flavor. Hit it with the honey-chili-vinegar mixture and scrape as it bubbles.</li>



<li><strong>Reduce the glaze until it coats the back of a spoon.</strong> Two to three minutes at a hard boil. If it's still thin when you add the pork back, the bowls will be soupy instead of sticky.</li>



<li><strong>Toss the pork in the glaze for 30 seconds, no longer.</strong> You're coating, not cooking. Past a minute and the lean meat tightens up and dries out.</li>



<li><strong>Quick-pickle the cucumbers while the pork sears.</strong> Five minutes in rice wine vinegar with a pinch of salt is plenty. They cut through the sticky glaze and refresh every bite.</li>
</ul>
</div></div>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">You get the idea…. So say hello to these Sticky Glazed Pork Rice Bowls and add them to your pork rotation!! </p>

Set aside</span></div></li><li id="wprm-recipe-47116-step-0-1" class="wprm-recipe-instruction" style="list-style-type: decimal;"><div class="wprm-recipe-instruction-text" style="margin-bottom: 5px;"><span style="display: block;">Heat the oil into a cast iron skillet over medium high heat. Season the pork liberally with salt and black pepper and toss to combine. Carefully add the pork to the pan once the oil is hot. Depending on the size of your pan, you might need to do this in batches to avoid overcrowding. You just want an even layer of pork so all the strips are touching the cast iron on one side. Let the first side brown, flip the pieces with a pair of tongs, and brown the second side. Transfer the pork to a plate.</span></div></li><li id="wprm-recipe-47116-step-0-2" class="wprm-recipe-instruction" style="list-style-type: decimal;"><div class="wprm-recipe-instruction-text" style="margin-bottom: 5px;"><span style="display: block;">Once the pork has been cooked and all has been removed to a plate, add about tablespoon of oil if needed and add in the garlic and ginger. Sauté for 30 seconds. Once fragrant, pour in the sauce mixture and bring to a boil over high heat, stirring frequently so nothing sticks or burns. When the sauce is bubbly, add the pork back in and toss to coat everything. The sauce will reduce to a thick, sticky glaze and coat the pork. Serve immediately over rice bowls with all the assorted toppings.</span></div></li></ul></div></div>

<div id="recipe-47116-notes" class="wprm-recipe-notes-container wprm-block-text-normal"><h3 class="wprm-recipe-header wprm-recipe-notes-header wprm-block-text-uppercase wprm-align-left wprm-header-decoration-line" style="">Notes<div class="wprm-decoration-line" style="border-color: #e0e0e0;"></div></h3><div class="wprm-recipe-notes"><div class="wp-block-group">
<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Cut the pork tenderloin against the grain.</strong> Look for the muscle fibers and slice perpendicular. Cuts that go with the grain stay tough no matter how perfect your sear.</li>
<li><strong>Slice the strips uniform thickness.</strong> ¼-inch strips at 3 inches long is the move. Anything thicker overcooks on the outside before the inside hits 145°F.</li>
<li><strong>Pull the pork at 145°F internal temp.</strong> Use a meat thermometer if you have one. Pork carries over 5°F as it rests, so 145 in the pan is 150 by the time it hits the bowl. Past that and it's dry.</li>
<li><strong>Rest the pork 3 minutes before glazing.</strong> Slap it on a plate while you build the glaze. Resting redistributes juice into the meat instead of onto the cutting board.</li>
<li><strong>Sear in batches no bigger than a single layer.</strong> Crowding drops the pan temp 100°F and you'll end up with steamed gray pork. Two or three rounds, even if it feels slow.</li>
<li><strong>Get the pan hot before the pork goes in.</strong> Cast iron over medium-high until you see the oil shimmer and just start to smoke. That's when you build crust.</li>
<li><strong>Build the glaze in the same pan.</strong> All that browned fond at the bottom is flavor. Hit it with the honey-chili-vinegar mixture and scrape as it bubbles.</li>
<li><strong>Reduce the glaze until it coats the back of a spoon.</strong> Two to three minutes at a hard boil. If it's still thin when you add the pork back, the bowls will be soupy instead of sticky.</li>
<li><strong>Toss the pork in the glaze for 30 seconds, no longer.</strong> You're coating, not cooking. Past a minute and the lean meat tightens up and dries out.</li>
<li><strong>Quick-pickle the cucumbers while the pork sears.</strong> Five minutes in rice wine vinegar with a pinch of salt is plenty. They cut through the sticky glaze and refresh every bite.</li>
</ul>
</div></div></div>
